2.text: Chukchee move about the country with their houses and herds. This slow

3.text: wandering is their normal state of life, but its range is not very wide, —

4.text: from forest-border in the winter, to the tundra in the summer, then back to

5.text: the same places. Longer journeys are undertaken with a travelling-tent, a

6.text: set of pack-sledges, and a small herd, which, after all, is but little faster than

7.text: the usual way of travelling. A single man, with a couple of driving-reindeer

8.text: and no luggage at all, may make a very fast trip of a hundred miles or more.

9.text: Then he must stop in the house of some reindeer-breeder and put his coursers

10.text: into the herd of his host, in order to give them a good rest. Thus the

11.text: Reindeer Chukchee, in all his movements, is closely attached to house and

12.text: herd. Therefore a man who has none, and tries to wander about with no

13.text: particular aim, is an “idle wanderer,” a kind of social outcast and pariah.

14.text: Maritime people are settled in permanent villages; and for this very

15.text: reason — that the villages are never moved — they have to leave them

16.text: frequently, and make long journeys in various directions. Moreover, they

17.text: live on the seacoast, and the sea induces the people to travel, and at the

18.text: same time makes travel easier. Many of them are given to trade, which

19.text: makes constant wandering necessary throughout their lives. Therefore wanderers

20.text: without any special purpose in life are more frequent, and are treated with

21.text: no such harshness as among the reindeer-breeders. Chukchee tales of Mari-

22.text: time provenience often describe a man who, from a mere desire to see distant

23.text: and unknown lands, has left his native place, and has gone far away. He

24.text: travels in summer with a boat, and in winter afoot. Perhaps this last is due

25.text: to Eskimo influence, because the Eskimo of America really travel afoot. The

26.text: Maritime Chukchee, in actual life, travel in winter by means of dog-sledges. A

27.text: man of a restless nature takes some five or six dogs, attaches them to a small

28.text: sledge that has been broken and mended in several places, and leaves his

29.text: village, sometimes all alone. With this sledge he goes from one village to

30.text: another, passes from the Arctic shore to the Pacific, and vice versa. In the

31.text: summer time he joins some large skin boat, going a hundred miles or more for

32.text: trading-purposes. Trading-boats, in summer, are often short of hands, and an

33.text: extra paddler is very welcome. While staying in villages, in the middle of

34.text: the journey, the wanderer may take part in some hunting-expedition, and get

35.text: his share of the booty. Some enlist on American whaling-ships, go with them

36.text: northwards as far as Point Barrow, and farther on, roam to San Francisco,

37.text: visit southern islands, then come back to their village, bringing no property,

38.text: and having no care of the future.

39.text: HOSPITALITY. — The Maritime people are also much more hospitable

40.text: than the Reindeer men. Each traveller passing through a Maritime village

41.text: will receive food for himself and his dogs for one or several days. No pay

42.text: is requested. Of course the traveller is supposed to have some wares or

43.text: provisions brought from foreign countries and thus welcome to the people
